new_statements.quote: No published description of Nokuku phonology exists, but my own investigation together with the sources listed suggests the following phonemic inventory. [p.25] ... Stressed (penultimate) vowels are generally unchanged except that *a > ɔ before a final high vowel: *damu > ʔɔm ‘yam’, *avi > ɔv ‘fire’. Pre-stress (antepenultimate) *a is assimilated to a following high vowel: to e when the following vowel is i, and to o when the following vowel is u: kani-a > kenia ‘eat (vt)’, *ʔavua > ovua ‘turtle’, *natu-na > notuna ‘his/her child’. [p.27]

new_statements.rule_in_words: At face value: the stressed vowel is the (historically) penultimate one, i.e. the PNCV penult, and antepenultimate vowels are pre-stress. But this is a diachronic statement about PNCV > Nokuku vowel changes, not a synchronic placement rule: Clark says explicitly that no published Nokuku phonology exists and gives no stress line in the Nokuku phoneme block (he does for Mota, Raga, Tamambo, etc.). Since present-day Nokuku has lost post-consonantal final vowels (p.27), the historically penultimate stressed vowel is now often the final syllable (ʔɔm, ɔv, perɔw, vetɔl), so the synchronic position is undetermined from this source.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress placement; the vowel changes are described as 'generally' holding, with dissimilation and labial conditioning exceptions for the vowel qualities.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, cited forms only (cognate reflexes drawn from Mackenzie's 1906/1918 translations, Ray 1926, Gordon 1889, Tryon 1976 and Clark's own 2005-2007 field notes). Family-level context, p.16: 'Word stress in PNCV was most likely on the penultimate vowel. This is its position in almost all daughter languages for which phonological descriptions exist, where the historic final syllable is intact.'
new_statements.identity_note: Nokuku = Nogugu (Ray 1926, Mackenzie's orthography) = Tanokuk (local name used by Taman, Taman & Rangelov 2025, c. 849 L1 speakers, Poaru to Ravlepa) = 'Santo' of Gordon in Macdonald 1889 (with 'Walua'/Valpei dialect forms). Lynch & Crowley 2001 (sec. 3.3.7) treat it as a dialect of a 'Cape Cumberland' language together with Valpei (valp1237), Tasmate (tasm1246), Vunapu (vuna1239) and Piamatsina (piam1242); Glottolog and Clark 2009 keep noku1237 as a separate language, closest to Valpei. All sources examined concern this same variety.

sources.note: Sociolinguistic survey: 'Tanokuk (Nokuku, Nogugu) (Glottocode: noku1237...). L1 speakers: around 849... Gordon (1889, p. 85-134) is a grammar sketch... A Tanokuk phonetic primer (Anonymous, 1870) has also been attributed to Gordon... Ray (1926) is a short grammar sketch. There is an ongoing project for the detailed modern documentation of this language.' 'The Tanokuk language documentation project started in 2024.' No phonology, no stress.

sources.note: Nokuku appears only as rows in the phoneme-inventory / POc-reflex tables and the comparative wordlists (collector D. Tryon); the 'stressed/unstressed syllable' footnotes are conditioning environments for segmental reflexes in other languages' rows; no stress statement for Nokuku.

sources.citation: Gordon, J. D. [1889]. Santo grammar and vocabulary. In D. Macdonald (ed.), South Sea Languages, vol. 1: 85-134 (preface pp. 59-60). Melbourne.
sources.note: Nokuku ('Santo', with Valpei/'Walua' forms) sketch: article, noun, adjective, numerals, pronouns, verbs + vocabulary; no section on sounds; no 'accent'/'stress' hit anywhere in the volume (two 'emphasis' hits are in the Efatese and Eromangan parts). Preface only notes Gordon's spellings I=ai, x=au, c=oi, z=sh.
